title: What If the Sky Went Black at Noon? It Did in 1780, and People Thought It Was the End

scenes.text: What if the sky went black at midday, with no eclipse and no storm? In 1780 it happened.
May 19, 1780, New England. The sun rises pink. By 9 a.m. the light is fading. By noon it is midnight dark.
Families eat lunch by candlelight. Chickens go to roost, frogs peep, and people pack the churches, sure the world is ending.
In Connecticut, lawmakers move to adjourn. One councilman refuses: if it is Judgment Day, he would rather be found working. Bring candles.
Rain falls black with soot. The dark reaches from Maine to New Jersey, where George Washington notes it.
The answer took 227 years. In 2007, fire scars in Canadian tree rings revealed giant wildfires in Ontario, smoke blown hundreds of miles. Not the end of the world. Just smoke.

description:
What if the sky went black at noon? On 19 May 1780, across New England, the sun rose pink, the light faded from around 9 a.m. and by midday it was as dark as night. People lit candles for lunch, animals behaved as if it were evening, churches filled, and in Hartford the Connecticut Council kept working by candlelight at Abraham Davenport's insistence. George Washington recorded the darkness in New Jersey.
In 2007, University of Missouri researchers found fire scars in tree rings from Ontario's Algonquin Highlands dating to 1780, pointing to massive Canadian wildfires whose smoke, combined with drought and wind, blacked out skies hundreds of miles away. Rain that day left a sooty residue that smelled of burning.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: In June 2023, Canadian wildfire smoke turned New York's sky orange in almost the same way, 243 years later. What should we run through next: a volcano that cancelled summer? Drop your own what-if below.
